_meta.title: AgriSense AI Tomato Condition Guide
_meta.publisher: AgriSense AI project (compiled from general, widely published agronomic knowledge)
_meta.jurisdiction: General guidance (East Africa context); not a legal pesticide registry
_meta.review_status: DRAFT - pending review by a qualified agronomist / extension officer

tomato_healthy.name: Healthy tomato leaf
tomato_healthy.summary: The leaf shows no clear signs of the diseases this model was trained on. This does not rule out root, stem, fruit or nutrient problems elsewhere on the plant.
symptoms: Even green colour
No spots, mould, curling or mottling
No webbing or insect damage visible
prevention: Scout plants at least weekly, checking the undersides of leaves
Stake and prune for good air flow
Water at the base in the morning rather than wetting leaves
Rotate tomatoes with non-solanaceous crops
Use clean, certified seed or healthy transplants
management: Keep up regular scouting and good field hygiene
Take another photo if new spots appear
get_help_if: New spots, curling or wilting appear and spread quickly

tomato_early_blight.name: Early blight
tomato_early_blight.summary: A common fungal leaf disease that usually starts on the older, lower leaves.
symptoms: Dark brown spots with concentric rings, like a target
Yellow area around the spots
Older leaves affected first; severely affected leaves yellow and drop
Dark sunken lesions can appear on stems and near the fruit stalk
possible_causes: Fungus that survives on crop residue and in soil
Warm weather with alternating wet and dry periods, heavy dew or overhead watering
Plant stress from poor nutrition, heavy fruit load or drought
prevention: Rotate away from tomato, potato and related crops for two to three seasons
Remove and destroy infected plant debris after harvest
Stake and prune to improve air flow
Use drip or base watering; avoid wetting leaves
Mulch to reduce soil splash onto lower leaves
Keep plants well fed and watered to reduce stress
management: Remove heavily infected lower leaves and dispose of them away from the field
Do not work in the crop when foliage is wet
Ask a local extension officer or agro-vet which control products are registered and appropriate, and follow the label exactly
get_help_if: Spread is moving to upper leaves or fruit
More than a small part of the field is affected

tomato_late_blight.name: Late blight
tomato_late_blight.summary: A fast-moving and potentially devastating disease, especially in cool, wet, humid weather. It can destroy a crop within days.
symptoms: Large, pale green to dark, water-soaked or greasy-looking patches on leaves
Patches turn brown and papery; white fuzzy growth may appear underneath in humid conditions
Dark brown lesions on stems
Firm, brown, greasy-looking patches on fruit
possible_causes: Spores spread by wind and rain from infected tomato or potato plants and volunteer plants
Cool, wet weather with long leaf-wetness periods
prevention: Plant certified healthy seedlings and, where available, tolerant varieties
Destroy volunteer tomato and potato plants and cull piles
Avoid overhead irrigation and water early in the day
Space plants and prune for air flow
Scout often during cool, wet spells
management: Act quickly: report suspected late blight to a local extension officer or agro-vet the same day
Remove and destroy badly infected plants (bag them or bury/burn according to local rules); do not compost them
Do not move infected plant material or tools between fields without cleaning
Control products must be chosen locally by a professional, because timing and registration matter
get_help_if: You see these symptoms on more than a few plants
Neighbouring potato or tomato fields are affected

tomato_bacterial_spot.name: Bacterial spot
tomato_bacterial_spot.summary: A bacterial disease that spreads in splashing water and is difficult to cure once established, so prevention matters most.
symptoms: Small, dark, water-soaked spots on leaves that turn brown to black, often with a yellow halo
Centres may dry and drop out, leaving a shot-hole look
Small, raised, scabby spots on green fruit
possible_causes: Contaminated seed or transplants
Spread by rain splash, overhead irrigation and handling wet plants
Warm, humid weather
prevention: Buy certified disease-free seed and healthy transplants
Avoid overhead irrigation
Do not handle or tie plants when foliage is wet
Rotate with non-host crops and remove crop residue
Clean tools and hands between plots
management: Remove and destroy severely affected plants
Ask an extension officer which bactericide options, if any, are registered locally, and follow the label exactly
Improve spacing and airflow
get_help_if: Spread continues after removing affected leaves

tomato_leaf_mold.name: Leaf mold
tomato_leaf_mold.summary: A fungal disease favoured by high humidity and poor ventilation, most common in greenhouses and dense crops.
symptoms: Pale green or yellowish patches on the upper leaf surface
Olive-green to brown velvety mould on the underside of the leaf beneath those patches
Leaves curl, wither and drop in severe cases
possible_causes: Relative humidity persistently high, especially in greenhouses or tunnels
Poor ventilation and crowded plants
Leaf wetness
prevention: Increase ventilation and reduce humidity in tunnels and greenhouses
Space and prune plants for air flow
Water at the base, early in the day
Choose resistant varieties where available
Remove crop residue after harvest
management: Remove badly affected leaves
Improve airflow immediately
Ask an extension officer about locally registered products if spread continues
get_help_if: The mould is spreading on upper leaves or fruit

tomato_septoria_leaf_spot.name: Septoria leaf spot
tomato_septoria_leaf_spot.summary: A fungal disease that causes many small spots on leaves, usually starting low on the plant, and spreads in wet weather.
symptoms: Many small, round spots with dark borders and grey or tan centres
Tiny dark specks may be visible inside the spots
Lower leaves affected first; heavily spotted leaves yellow and drop
Fruit is rarely affected
possible_causes: Fungus carried over on crop debris and some weeds
Splashing rain and overhead irrigation
Warm, wet and humid weather
prevention: Rotate crops and remove crop residue
Mulch and stake to keep leaves off the soil
Avoid overhead irrigation
Control nightshade-family weeds
Space plants for airflow
management: Remove infected lower leaves and dispose of them away from the field
Avoid working among wet plants
Ask an extension officer which control options are registered locally
get_help_if: Defoliation is moving up the plant and fruit is being exposed to sun

tomato_spider_mites.name: Spider mites (two-spotted spider mite)
tomato_spider_mites.summary: Tiny sap-sucking mites, often building up in hot, dry, dusty conditions. This is a pest problem, not an infection.
symptoms: Fine yellow or white stippling on leaves
Leaves turn bronze or dry and drop
Fine webbing on the underside of leaves or between shoots in heavy infestations
Tiny moving dots on the underside of leaves (use a hand lens)
possible_causes: Hot, dry weather
Dusty conditions
Water-stressed plants
Loss of natural enemies when broad-spectrum insecticides are used
prevention: Keep plants adequately watered and reduce dust
Check the underside of leaves regularly
Avoid unnecessary broad-spectrum insecticide sprays that kill natural enemies
Remove weedy hosts and crop residue
management: Remove and destroy heavily infested leaves
A strong spray of plain water on the underside of leaves can reduce numbers in small plantings
Ask an extension officer or agro-vet about locally registered miticides and how to avoid resistance, and follow the label exactly
get_help_if: Webbing is spreading across the plant
The infestation returns quickly after treatment

tomato_target_spot.name: Target spot
tomato_target_spot.summary: A fungal disease causing ringed brown spots that look similar to early blight.
symptoms: Brown spots with concentric rings and sometimes a yellow halo
Spots can join together and cause leaf drop
Lesions may also appear on stems and fruit
possible_causes: Warm, humid conditions with long leaf-wetness periods
Fungus carried over in crop debris
Dense foliage
prevention: Rotate crops and remove crop residue
Prune and space plants for airflow
Use base watering
Scout older leaves regularly
management: Remove heavily infected leaves
Ask an extension officer which control options are registered locally
Early blight and target spot look alike; a local expert can help tell them apart
get_help_if: Fruit is affected or defoliation is spreading

tomato_yellow_leaf_curl_virus.name: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus
tomato_yellow_leaf_curl_virus.cause_organism: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus, transmitted by whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci)
tomato_yellow_leaf_curl_virus.summary: A virus spread by whiteflies. There is no cure for an infected plant, so control focuses on whiteflies and prevention.
symptoms: Leaves curl upward and inward and become small
Yellowing of leaf edges
Stunted plant with bushy growth
Flowers drop and few fruit set, especially if infected young
possible_causes: Infected plants or transplants
Whiteflies feeding on infected plants and moving to healthy ones
Weeds and nearby crops that host the virus or whiteflies
prevention: Raise seedlings under insect-proof net
Use tolerant or resistant varieties where available
Control whiteflies and use yellow sticky traps to monitor them
Remove weeds and crop residue; avoid planting next to older infected tomato crops
Remove infected plants early
management: Remove and destroy infected plants early, bagging them before removal so whiteflies do not spread
Ask an extension officer about an integrated whitefly management plan appropriate to your area
Similar symptoms can come from herbicide drift, nutrient problems or other viruses, so a professional check is worthwhile
get_help_if: Whiteflies are abundant in the field

tomato_mosaic_virus.name: Tomato mosaic virus
tomato_mosaic_virus.summary: A very stable virus spread mainly by hands, tools and contaminated seed. There is no cure for infected plants.
symptoms: Light and dark green mottled (mosaic) pattern on leaves
Leaves may be distorted, narrow or fern-like
Stunted growth and reduced or uneven fruit ripening
possible_causes: Contaminated seed or transplants
Spread by hands, tools and clothing during pruning and handling
Survives on crop debris and tools
prevention: Use certified virus-free seed and tolerant varieties where available
Wash hands with soap and disinfect tools between plants and plots
Avoid handling tobacco products before working with plants
Remove infected plants and crop residue
Rotate crops and control weeds
management: Remove and destroy infected plants rather than composting them
Handle healthy plants before suspected infected ones
Ask an extension officer to confirm the virus, because several viruses and nutrient problems can look similar
get_help_if: You plan to save seed from affected plants (do not)
